review:
I hated to love so much about this game.

So much great stuff, I got really hooked with the duality of the situation as well as the strategical elements. It looked perfect at the start.

With a brilliant story and art, this game didn’t need anything else to be a success… except that someone had the brilliant idea to make the whole game about “beating the clock”.

I know some people are going to say: “So what, I like the challenge.” but some other people, like me, find this kind of game challenge the cheapest and most unsatisfying of them all. Much like jumping platforms.

A game this beautiful deserves to be appreciated, then absorbed while people play with it, not to be rushed through because there’s a clock ticking.

So if you like to fight the clock go forward, but if like me you don’t, stay away because that’s the core of this game’s gameplay.

Beholder is an interesting game that pretends to be more than it is. A simple gimmick of spying on people and surveillance, but with a minimum of actual interaction to go with it. After the first few hours, most of the game is about finding out what the developers planned for you to do and then following the story they wanted to tell you. If you wanted to just spy on people and have a few renters to keep an eye on, you're in the wrong place.

Mostly, Beholder tells you a story. And this story demands that you are a dou-che to everyone and extort them until they have no money left to give you before forcibly evicting them so you can steal whats left of their stuff and pawn it for spare cash. If you do not do this, you will either be given a game over or your family will die. Multiple times at that. In my one playthrough so far my son has died three times and my wife twice, forcing me to pay for five funerals for two dead family members. Through all this, people still threaten me with hurting my family which already died, and there is a good chance that if I don't go along with it they will dig up the body just so they can kill it again and force me to pay for another funeral.

There is not a lot of choice to be had, there are a few stories, and you have to just follow them. Some stories appear to have multiple paths, but in the end only a few seem to have any effect on others at all. Coupled by a world that appears to be intended seriously but comes off as a satirical joke where people try to one up eachother on cynicism, dialogue options being vague ("Tell me" -200 reputation- Could mean threatening them, right? Nope. It's asking nicely.) and the fact that you don't really get to do that much for most of the time except wait for people to leave so you can rummage through their stuff makes this more suited to something you can watch someone else play rather than something you can play yourself.

Aside from all this, I've found there to be some serious issues with Beholder, family members dying multiple times, the game not recognizing them as dead, the complete lack of manual saving, barely functional tutorial that doesn't even explain the basics right and very harsh penalties on what is essentially trial and error gameplay makes for a sadly unsatisfying experience where I found myself deciding that I was done and got the good ending after a bomb killed everyone in the building.

Graphics are simple, but they are pretty good at what they do. Renters are different enough to distinguish between them and the music works well for most of the game. I don't think it was entirely necessary to hear the basement stove turned on nearly all the time though.

There are good things to be had in Beholder, but it feels very much like they had a story and a single game mechanic planned, and then just jammed them together hoping it would work.
It doesn't, or not very well at least. The start of the game is fairly well worked out and entertaining, but then after that it mainly becomes a hunt for finding the right thing or dialogue you're expected to find while at the same time bringing in renters just to extort them for money. A routine that encourages you to not care about any of your renters, your family, or the game as a whole. And all throughout this everyone will stress how everything is bad without ever having anything good happen.

The game claims your choices have consequences, but the only choices and consequences are "Do as we intended for you to do or you and/or your family will die" with nearly no room for error. Even if you accept the loss of one or two family members you do not have many meaningful choices, seemingly by design.

Take that as you will, but I can not in good conscience recommend it to anyone but those who are the most hyped about spying on people while also being a fan of passive gameplay.

This game is fantastic. These days most video games are all the same, and whenever something new comes along, it's always nice to see. Like how we all went mad when the first few survival craft games came out, that is, until every single early access game became that and watered down the genre to the point it feels like any other. Beholder does not. Feel like any other genre, that is. The closest I could compare it to would be an adventure/point and click game, but that wouldn't be accurate. For starters, you can use a controller, and you can walk around. I honestly don't know what genre this would fall under, nor can I explain it good enough to tell you what you're in for, so I will just tell you what I have done so far in the game. 

I road a train into town where I was greeted by who I believe is the building owner. He asked me if I have ever run an apartment building before (I said "No (Play tutorial). I was then tasked with setting up surveilence cameras around the building, but first I had to get them out of my new desk drawer. After I set up the cameras, the man asks me to follow him upstairs, which I do, where he gives me a key, and privately tells me it will open any apartment in the building. He said to make sure they're not home when I enter, because "Citizens think their private lives are their business" (This is one of several great lines in the small amount of time I've played) and then you're left on your own to figure things out. 

I definitely recommend this game, if for no other reason than the fact that it's unlike anything you've played before. It's not an FPS, MMO, survival game, crafting game, strategy game, city builder. open world, RPG... it's nothing you've ever played, and for that reason alone (plus the fact that it's a quality game with good writing, excellent ambiance, and a whole Kim Kardashian sized butt load of charm) it's wroth the measly 9.99 they're asking for. This game is worth at least twice that. 

God bless Steam and their refund policy, if not for that, I may not have ever had bought this awesome game (the other was Darkest Dungeon, another fantastic game I probably never would have bought if not for Steam refunds).

Many are recommending this to people who like Papers, Please. 

Beholder gives you all the tools of a long term, open-ended game like Papers, Please and then fritters it away trying to create drama and tension unnecessarily. You will likely have just gotten settled into the game and the controls before realizing you've been playing it all wrong and need to restart - indeed, it is entirely possible to put yourself in an unwinnable state by buying some items and then not having enough to repair apartment 2 after you evict Jacob Manishek, the Very Obvious Tutorial Tenant. I had a perfectly good apartment 4 that I'd repaired too that I couldn't use even though all the game actually wants you to do is move in one of two new tenants.

Having learned your lesson and your way around the controls and game mechanics, you start again, get a little bit further, and are suddenly presented with two sheer cliff faces of dilemmas involving your family. This is not just a vertical wall but one that actually overhangs you by a significant distance. You need forewarning to even be prepared to deal with these in the time allotted. And then, even if you do, you are thrown a second huge curveball in one of them before the situation is resolved, almost as large as the first.

I have been reading walkthroughs trying to even figure out the first one, and when I saw the second one, I realized this simply wasn't for me. It is the difficulty spike to end all difficulty spikes. I speak as someone who played Dead Rising on the 360 a dozen times to get all the endings, items, survivors and achievements and say that this is worse. You need an absolutely perfect setup to get these things done; essentially, there is A Correct Way to play through the game and anything less will leave you feeling like you've failed or have somehow come up short. It isn't even that you failed as a player, you simply lacked a crystal ball to see exactly what was expected of you and were therefore unable to guide Carl to act with prescience, completely removing any tension or investment you would have otherwise had in the very intriguing scenario and story.

For that reason, I can't recommend the game. If it's meant to be an arty piece where you basically get everything thrown back in your face with a "ha ha, that's what living in a real dystopia would be like!" message then it succeeds. As a game where we expect to have the power to influence our own course and make a difference in the outcome based on quick thinking and skill, it fails.

With respect to Papers, Please, then: that game gave you obvious and logical clues as to what taking certain courses of action would have with respect to the storyline. Here you are suddenly thrown an unhittable curveball and told you're out if you don't somehow knock it out of the park.

Beholder is a resource management stealth game where you work for the government and spy on your tenants. You wait them to leave their rooms and search them for evidence. Evidence can be used to blackmail or send them to jail. You can allso deploy cameras to profile your tenants and gain money. There are many diffrent solutions to problems, for example you can completely ignore your family (Not buying medical supplies or education) and let them die. You can dig dirt or frame every single tenant that the game offers you, and let them die in their cells. The moral choises are yours to make. You can allso die of many things, for example: getting shot by your tenants, not co operating with the government, failing certain quests. The difficulty in the game comes from trying to balance government reputation (aka not getting fired and executed), taking care of your family,  having a steady supply of money in case something happens, and of course doing the quests in time. You will have to make sacrifices, like letting a member of your family die, sending a tenant to jail or not helping those in need. The game offers hundreds of interesting quests and is an all round full package. If you want a break from high adrenaline shooters and want a slightly slower paced, but still thrilling gaming experience, buy this game. I can recommend this game whole-heartedly.

Really wanted to love this, but found it hugely disappointing.

The theme, aesthetic, and some of the basic gameplay mechanics are really engaging... All of which means nothing when the  missions are so heavily dependent on trial and error - both because the consequences are entirely unpredictable, and the "optimal" decisions (which can only be discovered through trial and error or through reading the dev's mind) are the only ones which can give you a fighting chance of *legitimately* making it through the game.

I say "legitimately", because in all of your trial and error, running through the same actions and conversations again and again, you inevitably come up against loopholes and quirks to exploit which make no sense in the reality of the game, but help you to jump through the hoops it throws at you. The most obvious example is that the most signficiant challenges are the (often unreasonable) demands from your family ("Give me a huge amount of money/an expensive item in a short time!") - but they can be entirely avoided by simply ignoring them when they want to speak with you. If you don't listen to your wife telling you that your daughter is sick and needs medicine, then your daughter never gets sick... Ignorance or inaction protect you from any consequences (this applies in many other sitautions too - such as, if you avoid speaking with a guy who is furious and wants to kill you unless you pay him off, he will never independently take any action against you). 

Conversely, if you actually listen, and satisfy a dozen of your family's demands, it also has no real consequences. Acting early against the illness won't reduce the cost or avoid further medical expenses. Giving your son what he wants early in the game won't change his subsequent requests, or his reaction or the ramifications from any of your later responses. In this sense, your actions are largely irrelevant, which - in a game world which tries hard to convince you of its brutal reality, where choices should really matter - is a totally unforgiveable flaw in design.

This basic meaninglessness to your interactions undermines any attempt to build up atmosphere, and completely eliminates any emotional investment. This is ocassionally exacerbated by the somewhat clunky, unnatural English you often come across (non-native devs never seem to find decent proof readers), but more significantly by the blaringly incongruent, nonsensical conversation responses which slipped through the net - like neighbours chatting about your dead daughter as if she were still alive! This on top of the fact that if a tennant sees you spying through the door of one of their neighbours, or even running out of their own apartment just as they are opening the door, they will not react - only getting angry if you are still inside after they walk in (and even then, if they catch you and make you leave but you immediately knock on the door and start a conversation, they will act as if nothing happened).

And not only this slipped through; aside from the frustration at some of the missions giving you limited time to speak with an NPC who may or may not appear when you need them to, even in my limited playtime I came across a few missions which were simply broken and could not be completed, and it was these bugs which ultimately made me give up on the game.

Overall, this lack of polish in so many areas makes the game feel like a beta release, and the fact that the devs preferred to push through DLC and even move on to a sequel rather than addressing these issues erodes some of the goodwill I had for an indie studio trying to do something different.

Ultimately, the driving force for you will be protecting your family and yourself. If you want to play as a more or less moral character, this will be difficult to do. I should note, that the story gets very grim. Potentially every character in the story, including yourself and your family, could die. I wouldn't say it's as grim as "This War of Mine," but the closest to it that I've played. If you are a fan of political thrillers and WWII/Cold War history, you may enjoy this.

The atmosphere is unique and heavy. What about gameplay?

Essentially, the game is a series of quests without any hand-holding.

1. The quests are connected to various characters.
2. The quests are limited by time.
3. There are events that are happening on two "timelines": based on your current progress and based on current date.
4. There is total freedom with how you build your relationship with characters.


With these points, you will constantly shoot yourself in the leg: you might be too fast with your progression, and will fail a quest because the next point will be triggered too late in the game; you might be too slow and will miss the opportunity and would not even realize what was missing; you will not have a character that is needed for a completion of the quest; etc.

The game won't tell you what's wrong. Sometimes it's the not-so-obvious dialogue line, sometimes you have to steal, sometimes you have to blackmail, sometimes you have to be a friend, but most often you have already failed something without even knowing it. The game is flexible and it will allow you to fail.

This game design is clear: to "beat" the game you have to play it tens of times. You have to know the game first. Overall, I enjoyed my time with Beholder. Even so, if I had it to do over, I'd likely skip this one. The game has an awesome shadowy cartoon aesthetic, and characters (tenants) with intriguing personalities, tendencies, and back stories. It also has a fitting moody soundtrack, and some clever mechanics.

Soon after beginning the game, some issues arise with your family. These issues are pressing, and expensive. You can make money by taking advantage of opportunities presented by characters in the game, by selling items to a vendor after the government has outlawed them (creating an increase in value), and by creating tenant profiles or reporting violations by your tenants. Once a tenant is evicted after a violation, you can also confiscate all of their belongings and sell them, but I didn't learn this until a tooltip clued me in at the very end of my playthrough. Profiles were usually created by searching the apartments of your tenants after they left for the day, noting their interests and activities. I felt like there were times when I had accumulated a good deal of wealth, but I never seemed to have money when I actually needed it. Taking advantage of opportunities or reporting violations can give you pause, especially after you've gotten to know one of your tenants well.

After taking care of the issues with your family (or failing to do so in the time allotted), you continue to receive directives from the government and requests from tenants and those in the resistance.

The frustrating thing, for me, was in the mechanics of solving the issues that were presented to you. At first, most tenant issues can be solved by waiting for a trader to show up and buying a requested item for a tenant. Later, completing tasks can become much more complicated. For instance, one tenant requested that I get him some paint and a pair of scissors. The merchant carried the scissors, but I did not see any paint. After the quest had expired, I later found paint in my own apartment. I had searched my apartment completely at the beginning of the game, but at some point items were repopulated. It was not an intuitive solution.

On another occasion, I was asked to find a girlfriend for a tenant who was a doctor. I found a woman who agreed to meet him, and she told me to tell him she was interested and to give him a catchphrase of some sort to identify himself. However, when I went to talk to the doctor, the only option I had was "end conversation," and I never saw any woman show up for the duration of my playthrough. I couldn't call the woman back, and she never called me again.

At another point, I was asked by a foreign agent to lodge a certain tenant who would then somehow sabotage the government regime. I then lodged the only tenant I saw available. However, the only option I had when speaking with the foreign agent afterwards was again, "end conversation."

Other issues with the title include difficulty clicking on doors to open or items to search when you have the view zoomed out. However, it's pretty vital to maintain this viewpoint to be able to see when a tenant is about to return to their apartment, to avoid being caught snooping. Even with the camera panned out, menus continually pop up as you search and obstruct your view. Even trying to focus on the location of my tenants, I was caught snooping multiple times.

I installed perhaps 2-3 cameras in addition to those I installed during the tutorial (these seemed like they'd be a big aspect of the game), but they just didn't seem to pay off very much. I learned perhaps two extra facts about my tenants as a result of cameras I installed.

I felt like the game had a lot of potential to pull me in and cause me to ponder challenging decisions, but everything either didn't work like I thought it did or just went horribly. At the end of the game, my daughter was dead (this happened in like the first 10 min of the game), my son was in a North Borean (basically North Korean) labor camp, and my wife wandered outside during a riot and got herself trampled to death.

Playing Beholder often felt like an adventure game, with sort of obtuse solutions. For those who are interested by this premise and gameplay, I would whole-heartedly recommend playing the game "Orwell" instead.

Interesting Concept, Tedious Execution

Beholder immediately caught my attention with its unique premise: you play as a government-installed landlord spying on your tenants in a dystopian surveillance state. It sounded like the kind of dark, choice-driven narrative I usually enjoy. Sadly, the execution didn’t live up to the potential.

The atmosphere is strong — bleak and oppressive in just the right ways — but the gameplay loop quickly becomes repetitive. You spend most of your time running back and forth, installing cameras, digging through drawers, and waiting on timers. It feels more like busywork than engaging decision-making.

Worse, the choices that should feel weighty and impactful often come off as arbitrary. The game pushes you to make morally complex decisions, but then punishes you harshly no matter what you do. Instead of feeling like you’re navigating a dangerous system with agency, you feel trapped in trial-and-error gameplay that punishes experimentation.

On top of that, the interface is clunky and the pacing is slow. Even when dramatic things happen, they’re buried in a mechanical loop that rarely feels rewarding or immersive.

I really wanted to enjoy Beholder. The art style is striking and the themes are compelling, but the experience itself is more of a chore than a compelling moral challenge. If you’re looking for meaningful narrative choices, there are better games out there.

Every choice you make draws you deeper into the system, forcing you to confront the consequences not only for others but for yourself as well. The game’s style deserves special praise. The graphics are crafted with a unique, gloomy aesthetic that perfectly conveys the dystopian spirit. The music and sound design further enhance the atmosphere, immersing into a world filled with fear and despair. 

No matter how many games I play, I keep coming back to it, attracted by its atmosphere, storytelling, and moral depth. Beholder has become a timeless favorite, holding a special place in my heart.

I read the description and mistakenly assumed that this was an entry in the sparsely populated apartment manager genre, like One Piece Mansion or Unholy Heights, but with a more Papers Please twist of desperation and grey morality. It clearly wants to evoke that sort of sense, but there isn't any randomness in the tenants that you can take, and thus not in the freedom you have to behave as you see fit towards them, and thereby evoke a sense of grey morality.

So I restarted and tried to deal with the tenants carefully, to squeeze as much money as possible instead of shaking them down and having them arrested. This hardly worked either, and didn't add a drop in the bucket against the huge storyline expenses. Now, I'm reading that even if you pay them, it doesn't really help anything because the school closes & the daughter gets sick again. What's the point? 

In Papers Please you have to work hard processing people to try and save your family, and you actually can. In Beholder, you work exactly as much as you are allowed to and perform quests in order to burn money and get the next terrible event. It would be fantastic if it was a game instead of a novel you can fail at, but with no elements of randomness it feels like slogging through a particularly dystopian VN. Here's what to do: Make the negative events randomized or at least some of them, so things can come up that give you a sense of real desperation rather than feeling like the script is just cruel. Let the events pan out differently at random, so things can sometimes go well instead of always bad. Make a tenant generator that creates people who are randomized and not particularly important for any sort of quest, so the player can pump and dump them if need be. Make a real reputation system so that tenants care and remember about finding you snooping, or noticing that they've been robbed, and so their opinion will drop so far that might leave, confront you, call the police, or refuse to help you in events. Give the player a paltry income based on the number of tenants instead of making all his money through theft and spying, so he feels like he miiiight be able to survive without being bad, yet remains tempted to go immoral for his own sake.

In, again, Papers Please, you can starve, or have family die, or get arrested, or flee the country, or help a revolution. It seems like you can do all these things in Beholder, but none of it has any weight. If you don't have enough money, it's not because you didn't arrest enough tenants, it's because there aren't enough tenants to arrest. If you try to be nice to people, then that means that your daughter WILL die. It's not that you had a bad turn of luck and had to choose between your morals and your family, that's just what WILL happen. You won't have enough money, she's fated to get sick, she WILL then die. It's no longer a question of morals, it's just picking one branch in the story. There's no other way to get money, there's no chance she could stay healthy. Period.

In order to have desperation, you need to start with hope. In order to have hope, you have to believe things might go a different way. In Beholder, you can either let bad things happen, or watch other bad things happen later. You don't have enough agency to positively affect things, no matter how hard you work at the tasks, no matter how many morals you sacrifice, and that takes all the weight away from the proceedings. You're not having bad things happen to you, you're witnessing a story about someone who has bad things happen to them, and that's the main issue. Sure, some things can be changed, like helping the old man leave the country instead of having him arrested, but that's an expense on the establishedly limited amount of money you can possibly make, so it feels like you are just selecting one option from a few about what to make better. Do I want to help him, or keep my son in school? Which one am I watching this time? It doesn't feel like a moral choice to stretch your thin finances to help him, it feels like a decision between two absolutes, because in every game you will have about the same possibility to make money. In every game you will have both of these choices at once. So how is it different than clicking a button that says "help old man" or "help son"? Some events have non-financial ways to resolve them, but it will always be the same solution, talk to so-and-so and maybe give them some item, and that fixes it. Once you know, it's not a challenge of any kind, and you're once again just watching events unfold despite being the player.

This game came out when [i]Papers Please[/i] was all the rage and everything was about Soviet-style dystopias, but the actual reference here would be [i]This War of Mine[/i], a grimdark manager where you have to make tough choices to survive. At least that's the idea. The execution... varies.

In [i]Beholder[/i], you play as a manager whose job is spying on his tenants in an apartment building, effectively choosing their fates. You are constantly pressed by the needs of your family, so always doing the right thing — whatever you think it is — is out of the question. The right thing is very unclear, anyway: some stories do not have a happy ending at all, while others seem to, but in a dubious way (selling state secrets to a spy leads to an armistice, really?). As befits a game of this type, you can never truly predict outcomes, but generally it's about choosing between bad and worse.

I don't like how [i]Beholder[/i] is balanced. I tried to play it on intended difficulty, and I didn't hope to achieve everything I wanted, just [i]something[/i], but ended up backing myself into an unwinnable corner. And the only way out is loading an old save — thankfully, the game is generoius with them — and replaying a chunk of the story, sometimes making other choices, but more often just microing better. For some reason, [i]Beholder[/i] plays in real time, which helps with immersion, but means that sometimes you need to Click Well to get an optimal outcome. Replaying chunks of the game while trial-and-erroring your way to an acceptable outcome is not a fun way to deal with challenges, and the game, while not very big, is too long to just accept a terrible playthrough.

Another weird aspect is that most quests are timed, but you are almost never forced to initiate them (apart from some rare cases like a character dying due to another quest's events). So all too often it makes sense to let characters run around with exclamation points above their heads instead of churning through the story. 

Cameras you install are rarely useful — much less so than just rummaging through a tenant's things — but you barely spend Authority points on anything else, so why not install them everywhere.

Informing on your tenants is just... a mechanic. It's not choice-based, has no consequences, and the only reason not to write their characteristics is if you find this activity objectionable in real life. Which we all do, but the game does nothing to let you play out this attitude [i]within it[/i] — the best you can do is just refrain from using this (objectively useful) mechanic.

It might seem like I dislike the game, but I don't — not at all. All these imperfections mean little when weighted against the simple fact that [i]Beholder[/i] is a very [i]comprehensive[/i] experience. You're a bad person doing very unheroic things to survive, the people around you aren't much better, but somehow you don't hate everyone and everything here — the game is at times absurd, but often empathetic. That's just the type of people a dystopia breeds, and there are revolutionaries who want to change things... by only breaking a couple of eggs. 

No one is perfect, after all.

The mini-plots are interesting and the pacing is good. I think in the end [i]Beholder[/i] deserves all the credit if got, including a third-party triquel that seems to be terrible. That's real fame!

P. S. Is the rubber duck ban a Galkovsky sect thing or just satire? Will I ever know? Do I want to...?

For those of us currently languishing in the backsliding democracies that now account for the majority of the Western World, few games offer as much of grim and/or terrifying reflection of what may await us in the near future as "Beholder".

Set in a fictional recreation of East Germany (don't kid yourselves folks - that's where it's set) in the year 1984, players assume the role of a landlord who has been hired by the government to survey every facet of his tenants' lives so that they might be documented and then reported should any of those tenants commit "acts of sedition" against the state. These "seditious" acts range from anything from blatantly subversive behaviours like hording weapons and producing propaganda, to seemingly minor offences like owning blue jeans or even reading books. All of which when reported are punishable by the same fate - the culprit is beaten savagely by secret police and carted off never to be heard from again. 

So, as you can imagine, this game is a cheerful and lighthearted experience from start to finish. :D 

All joking aside, those prone to deep bouts of Apocalyptic foreboding and dread should probably steer clear of this game if they value their mental health. No doubt, the ever-present undercurrent of pessimism and despair featured in "Beholder" will at times make players question whether or not they wish to continue. After all, in this twisted Orwellian nightmare, there really is no salvation beyond the cold blackness of the void. However, as your efforts conspire to make your world ever more Totalitarian and hopeless, it gets to the point that even death offers no comfort. Rather, it begins to dog you at every turn as your small and unhappy family unit become increasingly vulnerable to the miseries of poverty.  

Perhaps the most shocking part of "Beholder", however, is just how quickly the need for survival can encourage players to indulge in divisive conduct. Often players may find themselves ratting out friendly neighbours, and even family members, for no reason other than the fact that they can. In the most extreme cases they might even find themselves purchasing contraband from the local fence for the sole purpose of planting evidence! Clearly, morality and honour have no place in a surveillance state. 

To be honest, "Beholder" doesn't really have any glaringly bad areas beyond the obvious foreshadowing of the bleak future that awaits all of us. Perhaps, if you have to name a con for the game, it would be that it possibly needs a little bit more variation in it's game dynamic, since it is largely a formulaic case of "adopt tenant - survey - profile for cash - identify sedition - report". No doubt, this issue will be addressed in the sequel that is already in the works. 

Do I recommend "Beholder"? Yes. Do I think it's for everyone? No. If you already feel that our world is turning into a police state, then stay away from "Beholder". If you think we're still a long way off from that living nightmare, then by all means buy it. Where do I stand you ask? To be honest...after all this time...I really, honestly, don't know any more.

Most of the genre in general, including this game, boils down to "Your child is sick" all of a sudden. "You need X amount for medicine", "Your child has needs that are very expensive, do you give them money?", "Your bills are here" etc. I guess I have complaints about the lack of substance in the genre in general, but also the game itself does nothing to innovate or improve upon these clichés. The game narrative could've been so much more interesting.

Starting from the writing/translations themselves - major grammatical mistakes, just very lousy, weak translations kill the narrative in its root because it does not make me the least bit invested. My daughter died? My son witnessed the event but when I interact to talk about it, it sounds like I broke the news to him, and also like we're just talking about some shocking event that happened, not the fact that our dear family member died?
The characters themselves... Our son is an academic, I don't understand why there is always an option to talk about mines, like it's an imminent danger, he doesn't work there at all. The game fails to give us at least a context in which we would understand the mines discussion. Also, is there literally any use for the wife or is she just doomed to be the housewife and constantly give us bills? So lazy. You're telling me all of the female NPCs, even the old grandma, still have jobs and work (except the prostitute, although she does, I guess, "have" a job), but my wife does not contribute in the slightest sense to our house economy? When the little ! appears above her head and it's different bills four times in a row amounting to around 2000 coins I just lose it. She talks about sending our son to work instead of college, but doesn't think about getting a job herself? Why are the currencies so large anyways? Big numbers makes it look like we are not that poor, mainly taking the currency as dollars. Why are we giving the wife 500 for groceries when realistically it should be something like 13.50, with appropriate scaling to our general budget, of course.

Many of the lines I choose to tell my family sound like we are strangers, like I'm angry at them, and I get the whole "it's totalitarian society ussr dictatorship bleak life no money no food everyone is stressed" theme, setting and genre, but come on... Completely two dimensional, boring, with so much more potential. It's almost like it's a parody of itself. "You have to answer government calls or else you will get billed!", "Crying/Apples/Jeans/Singing is now forbidden!", the police coming to take a dead kid body like they work at the morgue, the police in general beating up the first character we evict - the game just wants to show us how brutal and extreme the state is, but we know it is like that, we don't need constant reminding that it's so cold gray-brutal-bad-evil-depressing-totalitarian-bleak... We just know it is. Takes me out of the game completely.

The main gameplay is a bit confusing at first, took me two saves to understand it and be more efficient at it. I see everyone has their specific work hours when they leave by bus. Our character can't sleep. During the day he can explore their apartments, install cameras, talk to them if they are there, but what do I do during the night? I know, there is a fast forward button, but still, it feels like there is not enough things to do in the game but wait to speak to characters to continue the story. Why is there not a tab where we note their usual work hours? What if, on a random day, they come home late, couldn't that be reason for suspicion, also a nice game mechanic? The days feel like they don't pass because there is practically no day/night cycle. It's just one looooong night, I guess. There are basically no repercussions if other neighbours see us exiting others apartments, peeping through the door, or even if we are exiting their house while they are in the hall. But they do react if I try to unlock their door while they're home. Why am I renting apartments to new people, but I get no rent money from them? Why do I get paid only by quests and writing reports, the money managing system makes no sense? Why are there two types of currency, why are influence points used to buy cameras, but literally nothing else - of course, I can lose/gain them in conversations, but still, I haven't noticed a big impact, the NPCs don't change their opinion of me based on the points, or maybe I just haven't lost a big amount. There is only so much I can put in people's reports when profiling, there is only so much money I can get from that.

The economy system just seems broken. I don't know where to earn bigger amounts of money without just blackmailing everyone (which I can't do without having proof, which usually isn't there), but what's the fun in that? It often feels like the game is forcing me to play "mean". I tried maxing out my money on my second save, but I could get to maybe 5000 before my daughter gets sick and requires 20k for medicine, and my son, for some reason, has to donate 15k to his college (it feels like they wouldn't accept him at such a prestigious school if this is the family he comes from, how did the narrative writers think this made any sense?). Both (optional) bills appear at almost the same time. I'm not worried about choosing what to pay though, because there is literally no way for me to earn this money in the first place. I don't want to play evil, terrorise and blackmail people. The game shouldn't offer it as the only option to earn actual money. At that point the game just seems completely broken, and that's maybe half an hour into the game. Why are, all of a sudden, the costs just insanely high, before the game gives me any real source of income? It seems like a weekly salary mechanic, which we have to manage, with daily costs for groceries and sometimes luxuries and repairs would be a way better system, with also bonus pay from quests and profiling. Give me a way to earn the money you request of me by playing nice OR evil, don't force me to one choice just because "that's the point their world is like that totalitarian and bleak and harsh", so so so boring.

tl;dr
Seemingly broken, boring, lazy writing, mechanics make no sense, could be something much much better.

Beholder is a dark, 2.5D strategy game that has a highly impacting "choices matter" mechanic. Set in a Totalitarian State within a grim dystopian world, players become Carl Stein; the newly State-appointed landlord of a D-block apartment building located on Krushvice 6. Carl moves into the building with his wife Anna, daughter Martha, and son Patrick, whom he must care for while also completing all of the tasks given to him by the government Ministry, and tending to his tenants. Failure to follow the order of the Ministry, or even missing one of their phone calls, can result in immediate termination... aka, death. It's up to you whether or not you end up siding with and obeying the Ministry, whether you choose to be more lenient with the residents, or even eventually if you become a full supporter of the secret resistance movement known as New Tomorrow.

Installing spy cameras, eaves-dropping, going through tenant belongings, planting illegal items, blackmailing tenants, reporting infractions, completing both tenant and Ministry missions, and much more are all things that you'll be doing during your time at Krushvice 6. As with any other Totalitarian State, the Ministry enacts random laws whenever it feels like it, such as banning apples, prohibiting the ownership or wear of jeans, not allowing public crying, and declaring all non-patriotic music illegal. Needless to say, nearly anything can become punishable by law at any time. Carl will get missions from the Ministry often, with many of them containing time limits for completion; if you fail to complete the mission in time, you receive an infraction. Too many infractions will result in death, and death is a game over; reloadable from the main screen from your last completed task, however, as there are no manual saves.

Much of the little free time you get will be spent trying to make money and reputation, as both point systems are emphatically needed throughout the game. Money, above all, if you wish to keep Carl's family alive, pay bills, get certain items needed for tenant missions, and bribe your way out of messy situations. Reputation points if you want to buy cameras, repair kits, and convince officials otherwise of your anti-government deeds; if you choose to go that route. Money is hard to acquire, and you'll get very little of it by finishing tasks. Rifling through the belonging of residents and either finding illegal items, or planting them, and then using that information to blackmail them, on the other hand, can help liberate a tight financial spot or two. Blackmailing only works a few times on each person, however, and some of the more notorious tenants may just up and kill Carl instead of giving in. 

With that said, funds are indeed very scarce and you'll quickly learn that they become the main source of stress within the game. In fact, I would go as far to say as it's the center focus of Beholder; as it is the center focus for many of us in our real lives. After a little bit of play time, you'll end up being hit all at once with a very expensive illness, your son will need a ton of money for his education, and bills will continue to roll in; all while the Ministry is breathing down your neck to hurry up and do their bidding, and the time is ticking away on everything. The money system is an extremely crucial part to this title's mechanics, because without the factor to create an overwhelmingly stressful gameplay experience, the entire campaign becomes a boring drive through something that isn't very rich in its lore, or immersive in any other way. You'll find yourself completely drawn into the financial strain of the game, though this may also turn some people off, due to just how difficult it becomes; there are two modes to play on, one which slightly reduces the financial impact by a small fraction. Choices matter, and your family's life could be on the line.

The graphics aren't exactly anything to write home about, and for such a simple game with one screen, the visuals haven't aged very well; nor has the repetitive audio that consists of three or four brief tracks, with one main "rainy noir" style song that loops for most of a playthrough's duration. While the environment is supposed to be bland and lacking, given the dystopian setting, there's not really any visual stimulation within the game. This is fine for the first few hours, but when your playtime reaches the 8-10 hours required to complete Beholder, much less any additional playtime needed to unlock whichever endings may have been missed the first time around, you'll find yourself incredibly tired of staring at the same boring, small areas. With that said, the simple silhouette with white accents for character models are pleasing to look at, and they make identifying tenants and other people very easy by just glancing around the screen quickly.

For the most part, Beholder has held up well over the last three years. It still stands as a testament to unique and immersive gameplay, even if much of that immersion centers around financial distress. One playthrough is fun, but subsequent trods through the game may not appeal to everyone; despite the plethora of endings available, which numbers somewhere around 9-10. You do attain 3 endings at once, however. This release is also a bit temperamental, and for a while I did have issues with it wanting to run. Under no circumstances should you click while the game is loading, or it will just keep crashing. There are several other unaddressed bug reports in the forums, as well. Bear that in mind before purchasing, and hold off for a sale if you can.

Beholder took the silhouette language of Limbo, the morally compromised framing of [i]Papers, Please[/i], and the domestic management trappings of [i]This War of Mine[/i]. It then assembled them into something that looked rather striking but played rather thin. The stakes were clear enough, and the choices were framed as difficult, but the underlying mechanics were tedious and the outcomes disappointingly rigid. Despite the illusion of branching, the experience was heavily pre-scripted, which undercut the tension and replayability.

If you were curious about what might loosely be called the “dystopian government worker” genre, this was serviceable - but if you had already played [i]Papers, Please[/i], it was hard not to come away disappointed by comparison. Beholder looked and sounded excellent, but there was little here that felt original or especially considered. “Derivative” was an unkind word, but it fit.

One sour note sat outside the game proper. The developer publicly replied to negative Steam reviews, including plugging DLC on them. That looked bad. Creative work needs to stand on its own; rebutting criticism in the review space only cheapens the exchange.
In the end, this was easy to forget.

The Beholder is a hidden gem of a game. This game isn't obscure by any means but you really never hear about this game anymore, Except for its heyday when it first came out. To be honest I really didn't know what to expect booting this game up for the first time. I just though I'd get it because it was 83 cents and had spare change. I'll be talking about the base game and the DLC separately despite them being pretty similar with a few distinct differences.
 
The base game of Beholder starts you out as a landlord working for a corrupt fictional country. And you the player, Play as the titular Beholder, Carl, A landlord/security guard. Your job is to steal, bribe, blackmail, spy, and report tenants to make money and do the tasks the ministry gives you, All while trying to keep your family alive.
 
An important thing to note about this game is the time limits. Most tasks you can do give you a certain amount of in game hours to complete. This game does also have a clock for the in game days but it doesn't seem to have a set amount of days until you get an ending, though the ministry will call you automatically after a while if you don't ask for a new task. You can at least pause time to think through your strategy. All in all its not as stressful as some other games but I can see this being a deal breaker for some people. 

I truly do believe making over the hurdle of the stress really opens the other aspects of the game. The quests and tenants you can choose to house are really good. Each with different personalities, connections, and circumstances. One of the early quests is to evict the Schimmers by any means possible so you could wait for a new law saying reading is illegal and catch them with hidden cameras, or plant evidence in their apartment. Alternatively you can confront them directly and try to help them escape the country either by leveraging your connection to a employee who works at a cargo ship and smuggle them. Or try to retrieve the lost paperwork from a worker at the archives. all of the different ways you can solve the quests really impressed me. And while most of the ways involve optional tenants you may or may not have living in you apartment. You can usually find a contraband smuggler ever day with the items you need, For a hefty price.

Once beating the game I feel like there are two ways a player will approach a replay through: Excited and try to optimize how many tasks and money you can complete, while finding more secrets of the game. Or feel like the game becomes repetitive doing the same tasks again. I personally find trying to make the most amount of money possible very fun because trust me you need a lot of money to get some of the endings. If you liked something like Pikmin 1 or 3 I think this game would really click for you! To beat the game once it takes around 6 hours so you don't have to redo an insane amount on a replay. If you don't plan to replay the game then I'd recommend getting the game on sale. Me personally i went through the main campaign 4 times to get all the endings and achievements.

As for the DLC: Blissful Sleep you play as Hector the previous landlord and you have 2 weeks to live because the state incorrectly labeled your file as 85 years old. Which in accordance with the new laws Anyone over the age of 85 will be killed in two weeks. The game play is much the same as before, But I find seeing how the first tenants you knew from the base game get expanded as they had a great relationship with hector and even had a different family. The lore of the entire country and people are expanded a lot. The DLC is harder then the base game but its nothing too crazy. I do feel like in general the DLC has less ways you can solve quests in the game its more linear. But i think that's because the DLC has a two week limit whereas the base game usually takes around 25 to 30 days. As for the length its around 4 hours long at around the same quality of the normal game.

I think as a package the Beholder, DLC or not is a really solid game with a lot of charm and a unique setting. This game won't appeal to everyone and that's fine. But i think for the people who will like this game, this is pretty underrated! My final verdict is 8.8 out of 10. Thank you for reading.

[H1]The plot[/H1]
[b]Beholder[/b] is a game in which we play the role of Carl, and our task is to manage a building full of tenants in a totalitarian state.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The purpose of the game is to spy on and write reports and denunciations about the inhabitants, but also to take care of your family. We can also write blackmails on tenants, thanks to which we will gain extra money. How we lead the game depends only on us.

[h1]Currency[/h1]
In the game, we earn [b]money[/b], with which we can buy tools for repair or use them later on for various unexpected situations. Another thing we get for doing some missions is [b]reputation points[/b]. We can buy cameras for them to help us track the residents of the building.

[h1]Decisions[/h1]
Making difficult decisions will accompany us through the game. [b]Excessive decisions can lead to the death of a tenant or even a family member![/b] Throughout the game you have to play very carefully, save money, write as many reports as you can to earn extra money.

[h1]Difficulty levels[/h1]
[b]Trainee[/b] and [b]Government elite[/b] are the only difficulty levels in the game. The only difference is that the "Trainee" earns more and the penalties are less severe than the "Government elite" level. However, it is more fun to play at a more difficult level. The production presents us with quite a challenge.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
In Beholder it is unusual, the characters are black, and the only thing that distinguishes them from each other is the figure and additional attributes. Graphics does not scare away, on the contrary, is nice to the eye. Unfortunately, some animations are stiff, and the repetition of scenes, such as taking the tenant away by law enforcement, after a long time can lead to boredom.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
Through the whole game, the background is played by calm music which, after all, introduces the atmosphere of a sad, totalitarian state. It is a pity that in the game dubbing occurs only in intro and outro, as well as during the game when a car with a megaphone arrives.

[h1]Extras[/h1]
The only addition to Beholder's game is "Blissful Sleep". We play in it in the previous manager of the building - Hector, whom we have to save from the procedure of blissful sleep. In addition, there are characters from the main game, so we can learn their story. We can complete it in several different ways, on two different difficulty levels.

[h1]Summary and rating [/h1]
Beholder is a good game, placing in a totalitarian state introduces the intended climate, the reality of the country is strongly reflected in our character. However, after a several of hours of playing the game we are bored by constant writing reports and denunciations.

A fantastic concept that just misses the boat in terms of execution. There's a lot in Beholder to love; its bleak world is filled with interesting themes, its ideas about money vs morals sticks the landing extraordinarily well and its core gameplay loop has that Papers-Please-esque ethical focus that has made so many smaller games so ruthlessly compelling. The problem is that Beholder never feels as subtle or well-orchestrated as its central elevator pitch. Money isn't just hard to come by; it's nigh impossible to gather even if you were being the biggest asshole on the planet. The plot feels rife with bold concepts yet is hardly explored, with the ending cutscenes discussing overarching lore that's never highlighted throughout its story. Its save system is frustrating due to its constant and sudden game over screens and the core gameplay always borders on depth but can never quite manage to offer it. It's definitely an entertaining and noteworthy five-hour experience, but past that, Beholder feels like a concept demo for a much better game down the line.

Great concept for a game, very dystopian vibe and setting similar to "Papers, Please" and similar Indie games. Has some dramatic choices and different endings. Character's storylines connect with each other, so getting rid of one character might seriously affect the storyline of others. Some replay value (aka trial and error) to see the different paths...

HOWEVER. The game could've been so much better and suffers from 2, in my opinion, major issues : 
1. TIMERS (and THAT mission):
One of the earliest missions has you rushing to get $ 20k in a matter of a few days. If you don't, it has some VERY dire consequences that will affect the ending in a major way, no matter how good you do otherwise. Now, this is a LOT of money to make in such a short time, most people never even make that much until the end of the game. The only way to complete this mission without locking you into some of the worst endings is to follow a very specific path of ridiculous double-cross actions that immediately throw any notion of morals out the window. You basically HAVE to screw over several characters hard and metagame like crazy, all while under time pressure. 

Other similar indie games do dramatic and especially moral choices SO much better without railroading you just to avoid a horrible plot development that early in the game. Papers, Please and This War of Mine are good examples for similar games that do these kind of moral choices much better without having to create this forced tension. In those games, screwing someone over actually feels like a CHOICE that you may regret, and you will weigh your options for a long time. In Beholder, thanks to the short timer and extreme consequences, it doesn't really feel like that at all.

2. Lack of content/ Repetition:
There isn't actually much content here. You will go through the same motions on every character to get your money, and it will soon feel like a chore, especially if you choose to do the above mission. The only randomization seems to be placement of items, but that doesn't really matter. There's not that many characters and they are always the same, and most of them only have a fairly short storyline. You also won't be able to meet or complete storylines for a lot of them if you want to complete the timer mission I mentioned above, since character's storylines are connected.  If you want to see all the storylines, you have to basically doom different characters each time and see what you get from the other ones with trial-and-error. While this does reinforce the theme of "choices matter", some characters plot points seem way too dependant on other characters, and unless you CHOOSE to replay the game and work towards those storylines, you won't ever see them and they'll just be fodder for the machine.

TL;DR: If you like "choices matter" type games and trial and error, it's worth a playthrough or two. But be aware that it has a frustrating timed mission with extreme consequences at the start that might sour the whole experience for you, and that there is not that much content unless you want to replay and work towards seeing all the storylines for characters.
